title: Short Stuff: DNA Data Storage
summary: Short Stuff episode on DNA data storage. Josh and Chuck explain why archival data is kept on magnetic tape (LTO-9) and why cold-storage buildings are costly, then describe how DNA can hold far more data in a tiny space: a claim attributed to Los Alamos National Lab researchers that DNA could hold roughly the Library of Congress in a poppy-seed-sized amount, and a projection that humanity's data (about 33 zettabytes by 2025) could fit in a ping pong ball. They explain the encoding method, mapping binary pairs to the four nucleotides (adenine, guanine, thymine, cytosine) and synthesizing DNA from the resulting sequence. The main drawback is cost: a Catalyst-style estimate from CEO Hugh and June Park (as the transcript names them) puts DNA synthesis at trillions of dollars per petabyte versus about eight dollars for an LTO-9 tape, and writing is very slow. Josh argues costs will fall as with the Human Genome Project. The episode closes with a tease and sponsor/network credit.

segments.title: Opening banter and the data problem
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode and the growing volume of data that must be preserved.

segments.title: Archival tape and cold storage
segments.summary: Magnetic tape is the standard long-term archival medium, durable and cheap per byte, but cold-storage buildings are costly and tape's lifespan is uncertain, which motivates looking for alternatives.

segments.summary: Short break before the DNA discussion.

segments.title: Capacity of DNA
segments.summary: Chuck cites Los Alamos National Lab researchers, via Scientific American, on DNA holding roughly the Library of Congress in a poppy-seed-sized amount.

segments.title: Global data in a ping pong ball
segments.summary: Josh projects humanity's data by 2025 at about 33 zettabytes and says it could fit in a ping pong ball; the hosts joke about backups and storage conditions.

segments.title: How binary data becomes DNA
segments.summary: Chuck explains that binary pairs map to the four nucleotides (adenine, guanine, thymine, cytosine), and Josh describes physically synthesizing the sequence as DNA.

segments.title: Aside on Gene Wilder
segments.summary: A brief playful exchange about which content should be preserved first.

segments.title: Cost problem
segments.summary: Chuck contrasts an LTO-9 tape at about eight dollars per petabyte with an estimated trillion dollars for DNA; Josh cites Ars Technica interview with Hugh and June Park of Catalog on synthesis cost per nucleotide.

segments.title: Speed and outlook
segments.summary: Hosts note DNA writing is very slow, compare it to tape transfer speeds, and Josh argues costs will fall, pointing to the Human Genome Project's progress.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts tease the show's conclusion and close with the network credit.
